title: Why Convolutions?
text:
Why Convolutions?
Inductive biases
• Locality — correlations are mostly local.
• Weight sharing — one kernel applied everywhere on the map.
• Translation equivariance — shifted input ⇒shifted features.
Default stack
Conv →(Norm) →Activation →(Pool) →· · ·

Conv2D Overview

• Apply a local filter across the image.
• Same parameters used at all spatial locations.
• Each filter produces one feature map.

title: Conv2D: Single channel, single filter
text:
Conv2D: Single channel, single filter
Key idea
• Extract a local patch.
• Interpret the patch as a vector.
• Compute dot product + bias.
Mathematical form
Yi,j = wTxi,j + b
Takeaway
Conv2D behaves like a local linear model.

title: Conv2D: Batch processing
text:
Conv2D: Batch processing
Key idea
• Same filters applied to all images.
• Computation is parallel.
Shape
X ∈RB×Cin×H×W
Y ∈RB×Cout×Hout×Wout
Takeaway
Batch dimension does not affect the operation itself; it enables parallel
computation.

title: Conv2D in PyTorch: API
text:
Conv2D in PyTorch: API
Definition
• nn.Conv2d(in channels, out channels, kernel size)
• Optional: stride, padding, bias
Interpretation
• in channels: number of input channels
• out channels: number of filters (output channels)
• kernel size: spatial size of each filter
Takeaway
out channels = number of filters = number of output feature maps.

PyTorch

• Activation must be added explicitly:
nn.Conv2d (...)
nn.ReLU ()
Keras
• Conv2D can include activation (optional)
layers.Conv2D (...,
activation="relu")

title: Conv2D: Number of Learnable Parameters
text:
Conv2D: Number of Learnable Parameters
General formula
For:
nn.Conv2d(Cin, Cout, kernel size = k, bias = True)
Each filter has:
Cin × k × k
weights.
There are Cout filters, so:
#weights = Cout × Cin × k × k
Bias:
#biases = Cout
Total:
#parameters = Cout × Cin × k × k + Cout

PyTorch layer
nn.Conv2d(3, 16, kernel size=3, bias=True)
Calculation
#weights = 16 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 432
#biases = 16
#parameters = 432 + 16 = 448
Takeaway
A Conv2D layer with 16 filters learns 16 sets of weights and 16 bias values.

title: Conv2D: Receptive Field
text:
Conv2D: Receptive Field
Key idea
• A receptive field is the region in the input that affects one output value.
• For a single Conv2D layer, the receptive field size equals the kernel size.
• Stacking layers increases the effective receptive field.
• Stride changes how receptive fields move across the input.
Single-layer Conv2D
For:
nn.Conv2d(Cin, Cout, kernel size = k, stride = s)
Each output value sees a local region of size: k × k
Takeaway
Kernel size determines receptive field size; stride determines the step between
neighboring receptive fields.

title: Conv2D: Receptive Field Example
text:
Conv2D: Receptive Field Example
Case 1: stride = 1
nn.Conv2d(3, 16, kernel size = 3, stride = 1)
Each output value sees:
3 × 3
Neighboring output values correspond to input patches shifted by 1 pixel.
Case 2: stride = 2
nn.Conv2d(3, 16, kernel size = 3, stride = 2)
Each output value still sees:
3 × 3
But neighboring output values correspond to input patches shifted by 2 pixels.

title: Summary: Conv2D
text:
Summary: Conv2D
What it does
• Extract local features.
• Share parameters across space.
• Build hierarchical representations.
Final insight
Conv2D = local linear model + weight sharing + multi-channel aggregation.
